bibl.title: Microplastics in Seafood and the Implications for Human Health

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: human exposure to microplastics through seafood, and what is known about its health effects
span.quote: Because microplastics are associated with chemicals from manufacturing and that sorb from the surrounding environment, there is concern regarding physical and chemical toxicity. Evidence regarding microplastic toxicity and epidemiology is emerging. We characterize current knowledge and highlight gaps.

span.label: whether microplastics ingested with seafood harm human health, and what the evidence for that currently supports
span.quote: Shellfish and other animals consumed whole pose particular concern for human exposure. If there is toxicity, it is likely dependent on dose, polymer type, size, surface chemistry, and hydrophobicity.

span.label: a review that characterises current knowledge and names its gaps, written into a public-health tension: seafood consumption is being encouraged at the same time as this concern is being raised
span.quote: Nutritional authorities advise Americans to double their seafood consumption; however, awareness or concerns about microplastics in seafood could lead consumers to reduce their consumption. Research to understand and reduce human health risks is critical in order to simultaneously protect consumers and support their nutritional health.

span.label: critique
span.quote: Understanding whether microplastic exposures impact human health requires standardized and reproducible methods for sampling, exposure characterization, ecological assessment, and human health assessment. There is no standard operating procedure for sampling occurring on beaches, in subtidal sediments, in biota, or within the water column.

span.label: plastics degrading in the marine environment into particles that are ingested by the wildlife people eat
span.quote: Additionally, when plastics are exposed to natural forces like sunlight and wave action, plastics will degrade into microplastics—defined as plastic particles under 5 mm in size. This definition commonly includes plastic pieces in the nano-scale, < 1 μm in size.

span.label: narrative review of exposure and toxicity evidence, separating the physical from the chemical pathway
span.term: narrative review of exposure and toxicity evidence, separating the physical from the chemical pathway
span.quote: Because microplastics are associated with chemicals from manufacturing and that sorb from the surrounding environment, there is concern regarding physical and chemical toxicity. Evidence regarding microplastic toxicity and epidemiology is emerging. We characterize current knowledge and highlight gaps.

span.label: the polymer itself is described as non-toxic because it is unreactive and too large to cross membranes; the hazard is the NON-POLYMERIC fraction - additives and residual monomers - which leaches out of the matrix
span.quote: Once created, plastic polymers are described as non-toxic because they are not reactive and generally cannot easily transport across biological membranes due to their size \ [16\]. However, non-polymeric substances, like chemical additives or residual monomers, can be hazardous to human health and the environment when they leach from the plastic polymer matrix

span.label: degradation rate depends on polymer type, age, weathering, temperature, irradiation and pH, so `a microplastic` is a different object depending on where it has been
span.quote: The extent of plastic degradation depends on factors including polymer type, age, and environmental conditions like weathering, temperature, irradiation, and pH

span.label: THERE IS NO STANDARD OPERATING PROCEDURE for sampling on beaches, in subtidal sediments, in biota or in the water column - and the paper states this as the requirement for answering its own question
span.quote: Understanding whether microplastic exposures impact human health requires standardized and reproducible methods for sampling, exposure characterization, ecological assessment, and human health assessment. There is no standard operating procedure for sampling occurring on beaches, in subtidal sediments, in biota, or within the water column.

span.label: a top European shellfish consumer is estimated to eat about 11,000 plastic particles a year and THE IMPLICATIONS ARE UNKNOWN - the exposure is quantified and the effect is not
span.quote: Researchers have also estimated that a top European shellfish consumer eats approximately 11,000 plastic particles annually \ [23, 32, 37\]. The implications are unknown.

span.label: few studies have assessed how much of the chemical exposure found in organisms comes from microplastics rather than from other pathways, so the attribution is open
span.quote: Microplastic exposure also can confer exposure to associated chemicals. Few studies have assessed the relative contribution of microplastic exposure to additives or chemicals found in organisms, versus alternative exposure pathways

span.quote: Shellfish and other animals consumed whole pose particular concern for human exposure. If there is toxicity, it is likely dependent on dose, polymer type, size, surface chemistry, and hydrophobicity.

span.label: per cent annual growth in plastic production since the 1960s, against 5.25 trillion particles estimated in ocean surface waters
span.quote: Since the 1960s, plastic production has increased by approximately 8.7% annually, evolving into a $600 billion global industry \ [1, 2\]. Approximately eight million metric tons of plastics enter the oceans annually \ [2\], and conservative estimates suggest 5.25 trillion plastic particles currently circulate in ocean surface waters

span.label: per cent of ocean plastic suspected to originate on land, of which 75% is uncollected waste
span.quote: While some plastics enter oceans from maritime operations, 80% is suspected to originate from land-based sources \ [1\]. Discarded plastic materials enter the marine environment as trash, industrial discharge, or litter through inland waterways, wastewater outflows, and transport by winds or tides \ [4\]. Waste generation and waste leakage are inextricably linked and proportionally associated with economic development, local infrastructure, and legislation. Today, uncollected waste accounts for 75% of these land-based discharges, while the remaining 25% comes from within the waste management system
